value.overview: The Mangrove Rail (Rallus longirostris) is a secretive coastal rail associated mainly with mangrove forests, tidal channels, and brackish marshes. It has a long bill, long legs, and a laterally compressed body suited to moving through dense wetland vegetation. The species occurs in scattered coastal populations from Central America through northern and eastern South America. In Costa Rica, it is a localized resident of Pacific mangrove wetlands, especially around the Gulf of Nicoya.
value.classification: The Mangrove Rail belongs to the rail family, Rallidae, and the genus Rallus. It is closely related to other large coastal rails, including Clapper Rail relatives, and its taxonomy has changed as genetic and geographic information has improved.
value.identification: This medium-sized rail is about 33 centimeters long, with a long, slender, slightly downcurved bill, long legs, and a short tail. Its plumage is generally gray, brown, and olive, with warmer brown or chestnut tones on parts of the neck, breast, and flanks. The bird is usually detected by movement or its loud, harsh calls rather than by prolonged views. It often walks deliberately along muddy margins and among mangrove roots.
value.rangeHabitat: The Mangrove Rail has a discontinuous distribution along coastal Central and South America, where it occupies mangrove swamps, salt marshes, brackish wetlands, tidal mudflats, and channels with dense cover. In Costa Rica, it is a resident of the Pacific coast, particularly mangrove systems around the Gulf of Nicoya in Guanacaste and Puntarenas provinces. It is localized rather than widespread nationally and is not normally expected in inland habitats or along most of the Caribbean coast.
value.migrationStatus: Generally resident and sedentary. Costa Rican birds associated with Pacific mangroves, including the Gulf of Nicoya, are not considered regular long-distance migrants, although local movements may occur with tides, seasonal water conditions, and changes in food availability.
value.breeding: Breeding information is variable across the species' broad range. The nest is typically a platform or cup made from sticks, reeds, and dead leaves, placed on the ground or low in dense vegetation near water. Clutches commonly contain about three to seven eggs, and both adults may share incubation and care of the young. The timing of breeding differs geographically; detailed, site-specific information for Costa Rican populations remains limited.
value.dietFeeding: The Mangrove Rail feeds mostly in shallow water, mud, and leaf litter near protective vegetation. Its diet includes crabs and other crustaceans, mollusks, aquatic and terrestrial insects, leeches, small fish, amphibians, and other small animals. It may also eat seeds, berries, tubers, and other plant material. Foraging is often most noticeable at low tide and during the morning or late afternoon.
value.behavior: This rail is secretive, wary, and strongly associated with dense wetland cover. It walks through mud and shallow water, probes soft sediment with its bill, turns over leaf litter, and may catch prey in tidal pools. It can swim when necessary but usually moves on foot. Its loud, clattering or repeated harsh calls are often the best way to detect it, especially around dawn and dusk.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is not known with confidence and is considered to be decreasing, although the rate and extent of decline are uncertain. Costa Rican population size and trend data are limited.
conservation.threats: The principal concern is the loss and degradation of mangroves, salt marshes, and other coastal wetlands through shoreline development, aquaculture, altered water flow, pollution, cutting of mangrove vegetation, and disturbance. Because Costa Rican birds are concentrated in localized Pacific wetland systems, damage to important mangrove complexes could affect the species disproportionately at the national level.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore Pacific mangroves and associated tidal wetlands, especially around the Gulf of Nicoya. Support sustainable coastal development, prevent dumping and chemical pollution, maintain natural tidal flows, and avoid clearing mangrove vegetation. Monitoring records from Costa Rica can help clarify local distribution, breeding activity, and population trends.
